correctness.rationale: The congruence is reduced using \(Q^{-1}\) to one forbidden residue per coordinate. For even \(m\), pairing works because two forbidden conditions exclude at most two of \(-1,0,1\). For odd \(m\), one three-coordinate block has radius \(2\): when \(\ell\ge5\), the \(19\) zero-sum triples in \([-2,2]^3\) cannot be covered by three coordinate slices of at most five triples each; when \(\ell=3\), allowed two-element residue sets admit a zero-sum residue triple and the only nonzero canonical integer sums \(\pm3\) are repaired by replacing \(1\) with \(-2\) or \(-1\) with \(2\). Pairing handles the remaining coordinates. Sharpness follows from the all-zero forbidden profile: radius \(0\) is impossible always, and radius \(1\) is impossible for odd \(m\) because the admissible shifts are then all odd. The finite-set bounds follow directly from the same selection and the triangle inequality. The verifier corroborates all sublemmas on exhaustive finite profiles but is not used as an infinite proof.

value.rationale: The object is a natural quantitative invariant of a perturbation step used in a recent solution of a problem on strongly minimal asymptotic bases: the smallest uniform shift radius compatible with exact preservation of the total sum while avoiding one forbidden congruence per coordinate. The theorem completely classifies that invariant by parity and changes the source bound from order \(m\) to an exact constant. Its direct finite-set overhead changes from order \(m\) cardinality inflation and order \(m^2Q\) displacement to constant inflation \(3\) or \(5\) and order \(mQ\) displacement. The parity obstruction explains why the odd case cannot match the even case. This is a structural, reusable sharpening rather than a recomputation of a table or an arbitrary finite slice, although it does not by itself alter the main exponent range of the motivating paper.
